3a.say: Some information is **extra**. You can remove it, and the sentence still makes sense.
Test it. Remove my friend: Tom won the race. Still a full sentence. So my friend is extra.
Extra information is wrapped with a **matching pair**: two commas, two dashes, or two parentheses.
One comma is not enough. You opened the door, but you never closed it.
No mixing. A comma cannot close a dash, and a dash cannot close a comma.
Parentheses close themselves. Do not add a comma after them here.
Extra information can be long. The rule does not change.
Here is a trap. The opening comma is far away. Look back to see how the extra part started.
t: who had studied the volcano for twenty years

3a.say: It opened with a comma, so it closes with a comma.
t: who had studied the volcano for twenty years

3a.say: Extra information can also start the sentence. Then you need only one comma, at the end of it.
A real SAT sentence. A long extra phrase sits between two commas. Remove it, and the sentence still works.
t: the historic heart of Samarkand since the fifteenth century

3a.say: Summary: use the remove test. If the part is extra, wrap it with two matching marks.

3b.say: When a job title comes **directly before** a name, use no commas.
Putting commas around the name is wrong.
Why? Remove the name. Biologist wrote Silent Spring. Which biologist? We do not know. So the name is **essential**.
Essential information is never wrapped in commas.
But when the name comes first and the description follows, the description is extra. Use two commas.
One comma alone is a common trap. Use both commas or none.
The same rule works for any title: author, director, president, astronaut.
A real SAT sentence. Biochemist comes right before the name, so there are no commas.
t: how a bacterial defense system could become a gene-editing tool.

3b.say: Summary: title, then name, no commas. Name, then description, two commas.

3c.say: That and which both describe a noun, but they work differently.
That tells you **which one**. It is essential, so it takes no commas.
Commas around a that clause are wrong.
Which adds **extra** information. Wrap it with two commas.
Without the commas, a which clause looks wrong on the SAT.
After a proper name, the clause is almost always extra. The name already tells us which one.
Who works the same way for people. An essential who clause takes no commas.
An extra who clause takes two commas.
Do not forget the closing comma. Without it, the extra part never ends.
A real SAT sentence. After the name comes comma, which, comma, and then the main verb.
t: which was built in Samarkand in the 1420s
an enormous instrument for measuring stars.

3c.say: Summary: that is essential, no commas. Which is extra, two commas.

3d.say: Sometimes the right answer is **no punctuation at all**. Let us see where.
Never put a comma between a subject and its verb.
Even when the subject is very long. This is the most common trap on the test.
t: The number of students who joined the club

3d.say: Find the main verb. Everything before it is the subject. No comma between them.
t: The number of students who joined the club

3d.say: No comma between a verb and its object.
No comma between a preposition and its object.
No comma between said, showed, or found and the word that.
Correct: she said that it worked. No marks needed.
But be careful. Between two complete sentences, no punctuation is a run-on.
A real SAT sentence. The subject is fourteen words long, but there is no mark between it and the verb.
t: The large number of students who signed up for the robotics club last spring
the school to open a second class.

3d.say: Summary: keep subject and verb together, verb and object together, preposition and object together.

4a.say: The verb must match its subject. A singular subject takes a singular verb.
A plural subject takes a plural verb.
Here is the trap. A phrase with of comes between them. Names is not the subject.
Cross out the of phrase and read again: the list is long.
Do the same with that, who, and which clauses. Cross them out.
And with phrases that start with in, on, or with.
Singular verbs: is, was, has, and verbs that end in s, like includes.
Plural verbs: are, were, have, and verbs without s, like include.
A wrong version: include matches manuscripts, but the real subject is collection.
A real SAT sentence. The real subject is collection, which is singular. Cross out everything in the middle.
t: of ancient manuscripts stored in the library’s basement

4a.say: Summary: find the subject, cross out the middle, then match the verb.

4b.say: Some subjects are tricky. Group nouns like team, group, and committee are **singular**.
Each, every, either, and neither are singular too.
Two subjects joined by and are plural.
With either or, and neither nor, look at the subject that is **closer** to the verb.
Flip the order, and the verb flips too.
With there is and there are, the subject comes **after** the verb.
So there is with a plural subject is wrong.
In inverted sentences the subject is at the end. Look past the verb to find it.
Phrases like along with and as well as do not make the subject plural.
A real SAT sentence. The sentence is inverted. The subject, the fact, comes after the verb, and it is singular.
t: Among the most surprising findings of the survey
that most participants preferred printed books.

4b.say: Summary: group nouns and each are singular. A and B is plural. Either or follows the closer subject. With there and inverted sentences, look after the verb.
